claims.text: Mechanical twinning is the primary mechanism governing the dynamic behavior of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Mechanical twinning is preferentially activated at low temperatures and/or high strain rates.
Mechanical twinning governs strain hardening and energy absorption in dynamically loaded FeNiCrMn.
Twinning maintains a superior strength–ductility balance in dynamically loaded FeNiCrMn.
The FeNiCrMn alloy has inherently low stacking-fault energy.
Low stacking-fault energy promotes twin formation under high strain rates and/or low temperatures.
Mechanical twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The obstruction of dislocation motion by twins enhances strain hardening.
The obstruction of dislocation motion by twins enhances energy absorption while preserving ductility.
The contribution of twinning diminishes at higher temperatures or lower strain rates.
Dislocation slip becomes the predominant deformation mechanism when twinning diminishes.
High-rate and/or low-temperature loading will produce a significant increase in twin density.
Increased twin density will correlate with enhanced strain hardening.
Increased twin density will correlate with improved energy absorption and a favorable strength–ductility balance.
Under quasi-static room-temperature loading, the baseline alloy is expected to deform primarily by dislocation slip with minimal twinning.
The proposed mechanism applies from approximately −150 °C to 400 °C and at strain rates up to about 10^3 s^-1.
Outside the stated temperature and strain-rate boundaries, dynamic recovery or other thermally activated mechanisms may predominate.
Analogous behavior in similar alloys supports the proposed relationship between twinning and enhanced dynamic performance.
The quantitative contribution of twinning may depend on slight variations in composition or processing history.
